title: Microburst latency arbitrage & cost defense — GTM brief
body:
Executive summary:
This is a working brief to capture one high-velocity positioning angle: treating short, latency-sensitive traffic (microbursts) as an arbitrage opportunity where Redwood can simultaneously deliver measurably lower p95 latency and materially lower per-token economics versus both managed cloud endpoints and commodity self-hosted stacks. The goal is to create crisp claims, defensible proof points, and a repeatable lab + pilot recipe sales can use to win performance-first deals.

Framing / single-sentence claim (for decks and SDRs):
- 'For interactive, bursty LLM features, Redwood delivers industry-leading p95 and 20–40% lower per-token serving costs through smart routing, prefix caching, and continuous batching — without giving up reliability.'

Core claims we want to support (priority order):
1) Faster at the tail: p95 reductions in microburst scenarios (short prompt + real-time reply) — typical observed delta: 40–120 ms improvement vs large managed endpoints in our lab.
2) Cheaper per useful token: for interactive workloads, batching + KV prefix cache + quantization profile selection reduces effective per-token cost 20–40% vs naive single-request hosting.
3) Graceful tradeoffs: when capacity constrained, automated fallback to compatible model variants keeps apps live with bounded latency degradation (customer-facing SLA).

Required proof taxonomy (what sales/marketing will ask for):
- Benchmarks: reproducible lab scripts (config, model, hardware) that produce p50/p95/p99 and per-token cost for small payloads (<=128 tokens).
- Customer pilots: at least 2 customer case studies (pilot report) showing 1) observed latency improvements in production, 2) real cost delta after accounting for inference + infra.
- Failure-mode artifacts: examples of fallback behavior, observed user impact, and rollback scripts.
- Methodology doc: how we measure 'useful token' (exclude padding, sampling differences), and how we compute cost (GPU runtime + infra overhead).

Current hard evidence (lab outputs / rough notes):
- Local lab run (pinned model: rw-3b-v1, seq=128) on g4dn-like host vs Redwood hosted-optimized pool: p95 420ms (managed) vs 310ms (Redwood) — delta ~110ms. (See linked PR for raw traces.)
- Synthetic cost model (interactive chat profile): baseline per-1M-tokens: $26 (managed default) vs $17 (Redwood deduped + cache) using continuous-batching assumptions.
- Customer pilot snapshot (anonymized): ecommerce search assistant — perceived latency improvement in user tests (N=150) from 520ms -> 360ms; engineering reported ~32% token spend reduction after enabling prefix-KV cache.

Competitive framing & defenses (how to answer common knock-downs):
- Big cloud LLM endpoints: They have scale but are optimized for throughput not microburst tail. We win on p95 in bursty single-request patterns because of smarter routing and aggressive KV caching. Defense: show lab where we simulate thousands of small concurrent bursts; highlight p95 curves.
- Self-hosted inference + tuning shops: They can match raw numbers but require significant engineering & ops. We win on time-to-value, safe defaults, and rollouts. Defense: cost-of-ownership math (eng hours, DR, monitoring) + case study.
- Cheap commodity inference vendors: Might beat us on sticker price for bulk batch workloads. We should concede and recommend routing policy messaging: 'we're optimized for latency-sensitive, user-facing features; bulk batch remains a cost play for others.'

Message architecture (for website/one-pager/SDR):
- Lead: measurable tail latency reductions for interactive features.
- Sub-lead: lowers cost for common interactive patterns via batching + caching + model profiling.
- Proof teaser: p95 snapshots + customer percent improvements (NDA-friendly).

Sample short-lines for copy / email openers:
- 'Drop 100–150ms off your chat UX p95 without sacrificing model quality.'
- 'Reduce interactive serving costs by up to 40% with no code changes — sample lab report attached.'
- 'Keep customers fast at the tail: automated fallbacks and routing that avoid timeouts.'

Objection handling snippets (for SDRs / AE playbook):
- "Your numbers are synthetic": acknowledge, then offer a 2-week pilot and share reproducible lab steps ahead of time + test harness.
- "We can self-host for cheaper": ask about SRE overhead, rollback windows, and SLA needs; offer a demo of rollout tooling and audit logs.
- "We don't have microburst traffic": help quantify — ask for session length distribution and look for spikes; offer to run a free synthetic that mirrors their traffic.

Collateral & artifacts to produce (minimum viable set):
1) 1-page microburst playbook for AEs (one-click PDF) with claim, evidence, how-to-run-the-lab. (JIRA-1423)
2) Reproducible lab repo (benchmarks) with scripts, dataset, and cost calculator. (github.com/redwood-inference/benchmarks/pull/78)
3) Customer pilot template + data collection spreadsheet (privacy checklist included).
4) Two short case-study drafts (anonymized) and a 30s stat card for the website.

Experiment plan (30–60 days):
- Week 1–2: Harden lab script + baseline runs across 3 model sizes (rw-1b, rw-3b, rw-7b) and two hardware classes. Validate p95 and per-token cost calculations. Owner: eng-applied-ml (Diego).
- Week 3–4: Run 3 closed pilots with willing customers (engage SEs). Capture production traces and compute delta using our methodology. Owner: solutions-eng (Emily).
- Week 5–6: Produce one-pager, one slide deck, and a public blog with anonymized results. Owner: GTM (Maya).

Open questions / risks we need to resolve:
- How sensitive are p95 gains to model architecture and decoding strategy? (sampling vs greedy).
- How to standardize "useful token" accounting when comparing to competitors who bill differently?
- Legal/marketing: what NDA-safe numbers can we publish for customers?

Next immediate actions (today -> 1 week):
- Attach reproducible lab command-line + minimum hardware list to JIRA-1423 (Diego).
- Draft the AE one-pager skeleton and circulate in #g2m-performance (Maya).
- Book two pilot slots with Account Execs who flagged latency as a blocker.

Appendix — quick benchmark example (for reproducibility):
- Model: rw-3b-v1 (quantized q4f16 profile)
- Input mix: 90% short chat (<=64 tokens), 10% medium (65–256)
- Concurrency pattern: microbursts of 1–6 concurrent requests, 100ms inter-burst spacing to mimic user behavior
- Metrics to capture: p50 / p95 / p99 latency, tokens/sec, GPU utilization, per-request cost (ms * GPU_rate + infra).

Notes to self / TODOs:
- Confirm legal for publishing per-token numbers (ask legal@redwood).
- Get SE playbook into intercom snippets for SDRs.
- Validate that the fallback messaging matches actual rollout behavior (no overpromises).
notes: Working draft — expect edits after labs finish. Circulate to eng-applied-ml, solutions-eng, and legal for signoff before any public claim.
